Find the area bounded between the curve $y=\sqrt[3]{x+1},$ the $y$-axis and the lines $y=0$ and $y=1,$ as shown above.
after.worked_solution:
First, we make $x$ the subject:

$$
\begin{aligned}y & =\sqrt[3]{x+1} \\ {y}^{3} & =x+1 \\ x & ={y}^{3}-1\end{aligned}
$$

Now, to find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}({y}^{3}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{0}^{1}{y}^{3}\,\text{d}y-{\int }_{0}^{1}\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\frac{{y}^{4}}{4}|}_{0}^{1}-y{|}_{0}^{1} \\  & =(\frac{1}{4}-0)-(1-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{4}-1 \\  & =-\frac{3}{4}\end{aligned}
$$

We obtained a negative number because the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis. So the area that we want is $|-\frac{3}{4}|=\frac{3}{4}.$

after.problem: Find the area of the closed region between the curve $x=16{y}^{4}-1$ and the $y$-axis.
after.worked_solution:
First, we find $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{y}^{4}-1 & =0 \\ 16{y}^{4} & =1 \\ {y}^{4} & =\frac{1}{16} \\ y & =\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059137/assets/c1e092dd6302bb5948c6452e43b093fc3a531132580c1bb1e42fbe846152f63c.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=16{y}^{4}-1$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ to $y=\frac{1}{2}.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}(16{y}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}(16{y}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y-2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =32\cdot {\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}|}_{0}^{1/2}-2\cdot y{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{32}{5}(\frac{1}{32}-0)-2(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}-1 \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}

content.worked_solution:
First, we find $y$-intercepts of the curve:

$$
\begin{aligned}16{y}^{4}-1 & =0 \\ 16{y}^{4} & =1 \\ {y}^{4} & =\frac{1}{16} \\ y & =\pm \frac{1}{2}\end{aligned}
$$

Next, we draw a sketch of the region.

![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/question-capture/14059137/assets/c1e092dd6302bb5948c6452e43b093fc3a531132580c1bb1e42fbe846152f63c.png)

We want to find the area between the curve $x=16{y}^{4}-1$ and the $y$-axis from $y=-\frac{1}{2}$ to $y=\frac{1}{2}.$ To find the area, we compute the corresponding definite integral, as follows:

$$
\begin{aligned}A & ={\int }_{c}^{d}x(y)\,\text{d}y \\  & ={\int }_{-1/2}^{1/2}(16{y}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}(16{y}^{4}-1)\,\text{d}y \\  & =32{\int }_{0}^{1/2}{y}^{4}\,\text{d}y-2{\int }_{0}^{1/2}\,\text{d}y \\  & =32\cdot {\frac{{y}^{5}}{5}|}_{0}^{1/2}-2\cdot y{|}_{0}^{1/2} \\  & =\frac{32}{5}(\frac{1}{32}-0)-2(\frac{1}{2}-0) \\  & =\frac{1}{5}-1 \\  & =-\frac{4}{5}\end{aligned}
$$

Since the region lies to the left of the $y$-axis, we obtained a negative number. So the area that we want is $|-\frac{4}{5}|=\frac{4}{5}.$
